nameStory: This katydid gets its name from its strong association with salt marshes, particularly areas where spartina grass (cordgrass) grows. The species name 'spartinae' directly references this grass, highlighting how closely tied this insect is to its salty, coastal habitat.
description: The Saltmarsh Meadow Katydid is a slender, green grasshopper-like insect that belongs to the katydid family. Like other katydids, it has long, thread-like antennae and powerful hind legs for jumping. These insects are typically green to brownish-green, helping them blend perfectly with the marsh grasses they call home. They're medium-sized members of the katydid family, built for life among the swaying stems of coastal wetlands.

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found exclusively in salt marshes and brackish wetlands, unlike other meadow katydids that prefer freshwater areas or dry fields

idTips.label: Body coloration
idTips.description: Green to brownish-green with a sleek, streamlined appearance that matches the color of salt marsh grasses

idTips.label: Antennae length
idTips.description: Very long, thin antennae that are often longer than the body and feel delicate when gently touched

idTips.label: Wing structure
idTips.description: Wings typically extend beyond the abdomen tip, appearing well-developed for flight between marsh patches

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Moves deliberately through grass stems rather than making erratic jumps, often walking up and down vertical stems

habitat: Salt marshes and brackish wetlands along New England's coast, particularly areas dominated by cordgrass (Spartina species). Look for them in the transition zones where salt-tolerant grasses meet slightly higher, less frequently flooded areas. They're most common in protected bays and estuaries rather than exposed oceanfront locations.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs are overwintering in marsh plant stems and soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and vocal, actively feeding and mating among the lush marsh grasses.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, with females laying eggs before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity; the species overwinters as eggs embedded in plant material or marsh soil.

funFact: This katydid is essentially a living salt-meter for coastal ecosystems - its presence indicates healthy salt marsh conditions, and it's so specialized for salty environments that it can't survive in the freshwater habitats where its meadow katydid cousins thrive.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other meadow katydids, but habitat is the key - if you're not in a salt marsh, it's not a Saltmarsh Meadow Katydid. Remember: 'Salt marsh = saltmarsh katydid' - they're homebodies that rarely venture into freshwater areas.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'meadow' katydid, this species is actually quite specialized and doesn't live in typical meadows at all. The 'meadow katydid' name refers to the genus Conocephalus, but this particular species is a salt marsh specialist, making it somewhat of a misnomer for casual observers.
compareHints: Unlike the Short-winged Meadow Katydid which has reduced wings and prefers wet meadows, or the Slender Meadow Katydid found in freshwater marshes, the Saltmarsh Meadow Katydid is distinguished by its exclusive salt marsh habitat and well-developed wings. While other Conocephalus species might occasionally wander into brackish areas, only C. spartinae makes salt marshes its permanent home.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its meadow katydid relatives, the short-winged species is immediately recognizable by its abbreviated wings - all other Conocephalus species in New England have long wings that extend to or beyond the tip of their abdomen.
Among New England's meadow katydids, the slender meadow katydid lives up to its name with the thinnest, most elongated body of the group.

Among New England's meadow katydids, the straight-lanced stands out for its perfectly straight wing edges - the short-winged has wings that don't extend past its body, the slender has curved wing edges, and the saltmarsh is found only in coastal salt marshes.
